extracted.intended_audience: literate readers of The Spectator; authors, playwrights, actors, and general readers interested in literary criticism and social satire
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, periodical satirical and critical essays in the style of The Spectator: conversational moralizing pieces that mix literary criticism, social observation, and humor. Targets both composition techniques and ethical/procedural norms for authorship and theatrical presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in the sale of an author's work
rubrics_metrics.description: He ought to own all that he had borrowed from others, and lay in a clear light all that he gives his Spectators for their Money, with an Account of the first Manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should acknowledge borrowings and translations rather than passing them off as entirely original; compare authorship to trade practice—selling a product without disclosing its defects or provenance is akin to cheating the buyer. (Context: the author contrasts translating/borrowing with honest disclosure and pleads for authors to 'own' borrowed material.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of action, show, and dress in theatrical presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Advantages of Action, Show, and Dress on these Occasions are allowable, because the Merit consists in being capable of imposing upon us to our Advantage and Entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stagecraft—gestures, costuming, and spectacle—are legitimate tools when they enhance the audience's entertainment and understanding. Players' emphasis, gesture, and dress can make spoken words appear more noble or moving; such devices are permissible insofar as they serve the spectator's advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that performance can mask a work's textual merit
rubrics_metrics.description: They gave every thing which was said such Grace, Emphasis, and Force in their Action, that it was no easy matter to make any Judgment of the Performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and readers should account for the actors' power to embellish text: a vigorous acting company can make weak material seem excellent. Evaluations of a play or text should separate the merits of the writing from the effects produced by performers (example: the author's difficulty judging Cibber's play at rehearsal because the company made everything appear moving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade/commerce ethic: profit ought to be common profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Philosopher made it a Rule of Trade, that your Profit ought to be the common Profit; and it is unjust to make any Step towards Gain, wherein the Gain of even those to whom you sell is not also consulted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a moral rule for merchants (invoked analogically for authors): business should not extract unfair advantage from customers; sellers should consider buyers' interests and not pursue gain at their expense. This passage functions as an ethical standard for honest dealing in commerce and by analogy in literary commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical honesty: prefer ready-money trade and clear pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: He imposes upon himself a Rule of affixing the Value of each Piece he sells to the Piece it self; so that the most ignorant Servant or Child will be as good a Buyer at his Shop as the most skilful in the Trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete practices that promote fairness: avoid risky credit, use clear, per-piece pricing, and prefer ready-money transactions to prevent hazards to customers and to ensure quality and fairness (example: Mr. John Moreton reopening with friends' loans and fixed prices so anyone can buy fairly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody/mock advertisements and testimonials as satirical device
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of mock 'Advertisements' written in the style of newspaper cures and testimonials praising the Spectator volumes—e.g., 'Remedium efficax et universum', 'I William Crazy... have found great Relief from the two following Doses', and other comic testimonials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To satirize fashions, critics, or to humorously praise a work, imitate the form of popular advertisements and testimonials: use formal titles in Latin, mock medical jargon, invented patient-names, numbered 'Nos.' referring to prior essays, and exaggerated 'Probatum est' endorsements. This technique both parodies contemporary advertising and comically frames an author's writings as remedies or cosmetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise should be handled delicately (avoid putting praised person in confusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very difficult to praise a Man without putting him out of Countenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When praising someone (or oneself), use indirect, concealed, or diverting forms of commendation to avoid embarrassing the subject; the author shows this by publishing self-praise in a playful, disguised set of advertisements so that praise reads as humorous rather than discomfiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: On poetical justice: avoid introducing absolutely virtuous protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: There is none who in strictness can be called a Virtuous Man. Every one has in him a natural Alloy... I cannot think it right to introduce a perfect or a faultless Man upon the Stage; not only because such a Character is improper to move Compassion, but because there is no such a thing in Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragic (and heroic) writing: represent virtue as comparative, not absolute. Characters who are 'virtuous in the main' but possess some failing are more natural and more effective dramatically, because their sufferings can move pity and justify Providence. Absolute perfection is unrealistic and less instructive; flaws permit moral and emotional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy that shows virtuous men fall is often morally finer and more moving
rubrics_metrics.description: The Instruction and Moral are much finer, where a Man who is virtuous in the main of his Character falls into Distress, and sinks under the Blows of Fortune at the End of a Tragedy, than when he is represented as Happy and Triumphant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic effect: tragedies in which generally good characters meet unhappy ends correct human arrogance, cultivate pity and compassion in the audience, and teach not to judge virtue by outward success. The author invokes examples from Homer and the Æneid (Ripheus, Lausus, Pallas) and Aristotle's observation that unhappy endings were often preferred in contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both tragic modes (happy and unhappy endings) can be excellent, though ancient practice favoured unhappy catastrophes
rubrics_metrics.description: He himself declares that such Tragedies as ended unhappily bore away the Prize in Theatrical Contentions... it only proves that these are generally preferable to the other, tho' at the same time it affirms that many excellent Tragedies have and may be written in both kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary standard: acknowledge that while ancient and critical preference often favored tragedies with unhappy endings (they tended to win prizes), competent writers may produce excellent works in either mode. Use aesthetic judgment rather than rigid rules; the preference is a general tendency, not an absolute prohibition.
